news.title: Kamala Harris, Hillary Clinton, Oprah Winfrey and others pay tribute to Gloria Steinem
news.text:
Kamala Harris, Hillary Clinton and Oprah Winfrey are among a slew of politicians, celebrities, writers and activists who are lauding Gloria Steinem as a revolutionary and inspiring figure.

The celebrated author and activist, who became one of the most visible symbols and potent voices of the U.S. women’s movement, died Wednesday at her home in New York City. She was 92.

 Kamala Harris 

“To know her as a person is to know someone who was kind, sharp, and witty. She was invested in young women and keeping the door open for the next generation of leaders, and her advocacy was always about fighting for the strength, intelligenc, and dignity of women everywhere. She showed incredible support for women running for office, and I will always be grateful for her encouragement and support in my campaign for the presidency.” — the former vice president, on Facebook.

 Hillary Clinton 

“Gloria Steinem was, at heart, an optimist. Her activism was rooted in optimism, and that’s a moral choice she made every day. Even though we’ve faced setbacks to women’s full participation and equality in America and around the world, I want Gloria’s voice to remain in our heads.” — the former secretary of state, on social media.

 Oprah Winfrey 

“Every woman who has ever walked into a room knowing she belongs there; every woman who has demanded equal pay, equal respect, ownership of her own body, and the right to make her own choices; every girl who has grown up assuming that her dreams are hers to pursue — whether she knows Gloria Steinem’s name or not — is living, in some measure, inside the progress Gloria helped create.” — the media mogul and television producer, on social media.

 Nancy Pelosi 

“May it be a comfort to all of us who loved Gloria that her extraordinary legacy will live on in every generation that carries her fight forward.” — former Speaker of the House, on X.

 Jane Fonda 

“For decades, she trudged through every airport in the country, in sandals and a trench, carrying her own suitcase, packed with a few black clothes, hair curlers, and steam iron, in order to speak to women — at conferences, town halls, consciousness raising groups. No group was too small to deserve Gloria’s time. This is how she built the new women’s movement.” — actor and activist, on Instagram.

 Barbra Streisand 

“From the first moment I met Gloria in the 1970s, I was deeply impressed by her. She stood for everything I believed in: equality for women in the workplace, a woman’s right to choose, greater political representation for women, and a thoughtful, determined response to every form of gender-based discrimination. She gave voice to these issues with fierce intelligence and steely determination, but also with wit, empathy, and humility. What made her so extraordinary was not only the strength of her convictions, but the humanity and grace with which she expressed them.” — singer and actor, on social media.

 Jill Biden 

“Gloria Steinem understood that women’s equality begins with the freedom to make decisions about our own bodies, health, and futures. For decades, she fought to make that freedom real for generations of women and girls. She spoke up when it was difficult, listened to those whose voices too often went unheard, and never stopped pushing our country forward.” — the former first lady, on social media.

 Melinda French Gates 

“Generational change doesn’t happen by accident or fate — it takes leaders like Gloria Steinem who work hand in hand with so many others to build a lasting movement.. What a light she was for me and so many others. What a debt we owe her.” — the philanthropist and businesswoman, on social media.

 Julie Taymor 

“She got tremendous joy out of being with other people, with other women, and improving their lives. ... She understood about working from the bottom up — and she never really wanted credit for any of it. She always said if she wasn’t alive, there would still be a women’s movement. I think she underestimated her power. She was very modest. She had not an ounce of, you know, narcissism or ‘me, me, me’ about her. And she was able to really make change.” — the director of “The Glorias,” a 2020 biopic of Steinem, in an interview with The Associated Press.

 Julianne Moore 

“The time I spent studying Gloria Steinem in order to play her was one of the most edifying of my life. Everything I watched, everything I read, everything I observed about her gave me a template for how I wanted to behave.” — the actor, who played Steinem in the 2020 film “The Glorias,” on Instagram.

 Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex 

“Privately, she was even better than you would imagine — spending Thanksgiving with our family, introducing me to one of my best friends (forever the champion of female friendship), loving our children with her whole heart, counseling me during hard times, and giving extraordinary advice and perspective with a cup of tea and an unrivaled cheekiness and wit.” — Duchess of Sussex, on Instagram.

 Roxane Gay 

“Gloria was one of a kind. Genuine, generous, curious, thoughtful. She lived a staggering life and her passing is a staggering loss tempered only by the ferocity of her legacy.” — the writer, on Instagram.

 Abigail Disney 

“Everything Gloria did was rooted in kindness. It flowed through her political activism.” — her friend and fellow activist, to the AP.

 Rachel Cargle 

“Gloria, you changed my life. You seeded a fire in me that would result in my own activism. I am forever grateful to have learned from what you offered the world.” — the author and social justice activist, commenting on Instagram.

 Harvey Fierstein 

“An unstoppable visionary who demanded an equal role for females in a male dominated world and worked tirelessly, for decades, to bring that change about. The greatest irony was how many women she had to battle as they cowered behind their male owners. But battle she did. Equal rights! Freedom to choose! Access to political power! Equal pay for equal effort.” — the actor and playwright, on social media. 

 Jill Filipovic 

“I have done what I wanted to do with my life. That would not have been possible without Steinem and the scores of other feminists who it is no exaggeration to say radically reshaped America and the world.” — the author and feminist, in her Substack newsletter.
news.summary: Kamala Harris, Hillary Clinton and Oprah Winfrey are among a slew of politicians, celebrities, writers and activists who are lauding Gloria Steinem as a revolutionary and inspiring figure

House Speaker Mike Johnson already knows what the Republican-dominated Supreme Court is in for when Democrats get big-enough control of Congress and the White House, writes Slate’s Alexis Romero. That’s why Johnson tried to pass a new law out of the House to stop it.

“Johnson … led an effort Wednesday to amend the Constitution and cap the number of Supreme Court justices at nine. Since the size of the court is currently set by federal law, not by the Constitution, Johnson said the amendment was necessary to stop Democrats from adding justices to the court,” wrote Romero. “Over the course of 24 hours, Johnson announced his plan to introduce the amendment and had it brought to the House floor, only for it to immediately fail along party lines.”

President Donald Trump has been having a bit of a romp lately with his tailor-made Republican Supreme Court imparting huge new power to the executive and legal immunity for Trump to do as he wills with state agencies, immigration and the very face of Washington DC., and the White House. Romero said “it doesn’t take a brain surgeon (or even a lawyer) to understand why the leader of the House GOP would like to keep in place a Supreme Court with six Republican appointees,” but he added that these kinds of legislative efforts are extremely rare coming from any speaker.

But New York Times columnist Jamelle Bouie pointed out that “Democrats are getting serious about court reform.” Former Vice President and Democratic nominee Kamala Harris also officially advocated for expanding the court from nine to 13 justices because the country already has 13 intermediate courts of appeal and a 13-member Supreme Court would allow each justice to review motions from a lower court one-to-one.

But Johnson wants Congressional Republicans to jettison the power to expand the court before Democrats use it to neutralize the conservative majority that granted Trump immunity from crimes while in the White House and nearly removed Constitutional birthright citizenship.

Romero called it an extreme bid by the Speaker for “constitutional self-castration.”

“But Republican legislators would rather sabotage their own chamber’s constitutional authority than allow Democrats the chance to reform the court,” said Romero. “In opposition to Johnson’s proposal, House Minority Whip Katherine Clark noted that the amendment would strip Congress of ‘yet another constitutional authority that is meant to be controlled by the American people’s representatives.’”

“Think for a second about the moral calculus the GOP is doing,” urged Romero. “We’re talking about a system of congressional authority over the court that has lasted for 250 years. And Republicans are so scared of the electorate voting for judicial reform that they would eliminate a key piece of that century-old authority in the two months before they’re likely voted out of office.”

But the court-reform debate is raging, said Romero, because the nation’s high court is deeply detached from the public. It is a court that “avoids contending with ethics complaints against its own members, while blessing ethical violations in the White House.” Its judges demand the privacy of no cameras in its chambers, while allowing states to “invade the private medical decisions of women across the country,” he said. It’s also a court that “anonymously votes behind closed doors in secret rulings, and does so in support of Trump’s not-so-secret effort to disenfranchise votes by mail.”

“Until all of that changes, court reform will be top of mind and top of discussion, no matter what the Republicans try to do before November,” Romero assured.

news.title: Stop the Democrats’ scheme to pack the Supreme Court
news.text:
Democrats are in a quandary over the Supreme Court. Every four years, they’ve warned their voters that electing a Republican president will lead to more conservative Supreme Court justices. And yet since Ronald Reagan’s election in 1980 through today, they’ve lost more presidential elections than they’ve won. Maybe the voters are telling Democrats something. Maybe Americans don’t want the court packed with Sonia Sotomayors who make up or rewrite the laws as they see fit.

So now the left is angry over the tilt of the court, which has six conservatives and three liberals.

Why? Because elections have consequences. Sorry, this is the price you pay for nominating Michael Dukakis, John Kerry, Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris. They aren’t exactly hanging around anywhere near the 50-yard line on political ideology.

Now we have Democrats divided on what to do next. Many want Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez or Elizabeth Warren to be their next presidential nominee. There’s no learning curve here.

In the meantime, while Donald Trump is still president, they want urgent action. On the one hand, the democratic socialists want to abolish the highest court of the land. What they want to replace it with is anyone’s guess.

Other party leaders want to pack the court with four new liberal justices. Franklin Roosevelt tried this court-packing scheme in 1937, and voters rebelled.

But here they go again. On Sunday, Rep. James Clyburn, D-S.C., raised this possibility and disgracefully played the race card when asked about the Supreme Court’s recent decisions. He accused Republicans of taking “this country back … to those rulings of Justice Taney that said, ‘No black man has any right that a white man must respect.'” He was referring to Supreme Court Justice Roger Taney, who wrote the infamous 1857 Dred Scott opinion just before the Civil War.

Does he even know that for 100 years after the Civil War, Democrats were the party of segregation?

What’s deeply troubling about this war on the Supreme Court is that this is the institution that is the final check against runaway mob-rule democracy that can trample the rights of the minority. That minority could be blacks, Hispanics, gays, immigrants or disabled people. They don’t seem to understand that pure majority-rule democracy is, as the old saying goes, two wolves and a sheep voting on what to have for dinner.

Pure democracy only goes your way until you no longer have 50% plus one voters on your side. Clyburn is right that there have been occasions, like the one from 1857 that he mentioned, when the court has made egregiously wrong decisions. But mostly, the court gets it right. It’s not clear how stacking the court – on the left or the right – could make for more just decisions.

This is why Republicans are so wrong to try to abolish the filibusters in the Senate. We always want to make it HARDER, not easier, to pass new edicts that impair our freedoms.

I, personally, would have no problem expanding the Supreme Court to 12 justices if it could be done in a fair, nonpartisan way. I also strongly support a mandatory retirement age of 75 for all future justices on the court.

But to overly politicize – or, worse, do away with – the Supreme Court and allow Congress to have the last word on the constitutionality of new laws is a dangerous proposition. James Madison once famously described the judiciary as a “bulwark” of our liberties. Hopefully, we will never give up this most important check and balance on runaway government power.

news.title: Kamala Harris Faces Fact Democrats Are Telling Her 'No Thanks'
news.text:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris was forced to face reports about other Democrats rebuffing her campaign help this midterm cycle.

While paying tribute to feminist activist Gloria Steinem Thursday on MS NOW, “State of Play” host Peter Alexander asked the 2024 presidential candidate about a Politico story citing a range of Democratic candidates in red states and rural areas who want her to stay away from their races or have flat-out rejected her endorsement offers.

Harris responded, “Listen, Peter, we need to win, OK? Bottom line, we need to win. I have run locally, I’ve run for statewide office, and obviously nationally.”

Though she made sure to highlight her campaign credentials, the California-bred politician said she’ll defer to the candidates who “know what they need to do to win, and I would expect nothing less.”

Either way, Harris said, electing Democrats who will curb President Donald Trump and the Republican Party’s power is her main goal.

She told Alexander, “I look forward to being on the trail and helping folks where I can be helpful, but we have got to put a check on this lawless administration and deliver what Americans need and deserve: lower costs, affordable healthcare, affordable childcare, you name it. So I support them in doing whatever they need to do to win.”

Sources both on and off the record in the Politico piece said they wanted to focus on local politics and weren’t interested in any assists from national-level Democrats.

Senate nominee Adam Hamilton, a Kansas Democrat, put things frankly for Politico, saying, “Having somebody from California come in and try to tell Kansans who they should vote for is a pretty bad idea.”

Reynolds was talking about an upcoming film that focuses heavily on American culture in the 1980s when he described what he thinks the decade was really about.

'Sociopolitical tensions everywhere.'

Speaking to a reporter from the red carpet, Reynolds said that looking back at the 1980s now, the decade tends to be seen through rose-colored glasses and not for how it actually was.

"What's interesting about when you get far enough away from a time period that's quite distinct, I think there's always a lovely feeling associated with it. It's almost like you pave over all the trauma with, like, puppy dogs and ice cream," the actor began. "The '80s was a brutal, brutal time for people. It was a f**king mess."

Reynolds was born in Vancouver, Canada, in 1976 and grew up in the province. Now 49, he described the American 1980s as being filled with political tensions.

"It was a tremendous strife," he told Variety. "Sociopolitical tensions everywhere. We were still pretty fresh off a Cuban missile crisis, which was only like 15-20 years before. It’s a tumultuous period, but you look back at it now and you’re like, 'Oh, yeah. "Top Gun." Cocaine!' Like, no! It was really scary."

Author Sarah Adams added, "The 80s were amazing, what the hell is this revisionist history."

At least one reader agreed with Reynolds, though, pointing to '80s issues like peer pressure and divorce.

This, along with AIDS, serves as the true reality of the time, Reynolds explained.

"I think when you look back at 2026 and this era, I think they're going to pick on the big-ticket items that don't really leave the footprint culturally that you would think it would. I don't know. ... I wonder what it's going to be. Is going to be like, 'Oh, the COVID era' or something. I have no idea," Reynolds concluded.

news.title: Chuck Schumer Dealt Warning Sign About AOC Challenge in New Poll
news.text: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer received another warning sign about his popularity relative to Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez among New York voters, as the progressive congresswoman has been floated as a potential challenger ahead of his 2028 reelection. Ocasio-Cortez, who represents parts of Queens and the Bronx in the House of Representatives, is seen as a new leader of the progressive movement, which gained significant ground in New York during this year’s Democratic primaries. Her next steps will be closely watched over the coming months, as some Democrats expect she will either run for president or challenge Schumer for his Senate seat. Some progressives view her as the best choice for the left in the 2028 presidential race, as it’s not clear who else could occupy the left-leaning lane in the Democratic primary; but others believe she should run for Senate against Schumer, whose popularity has waned as Democratic voters are frustrated with what they view as a lethargic approach to President Donald Trump’s administration. AOC More Popular Than Schumer in New York, Poll Finds A new poll released Thursday by the organization Education Reform Now Advocacy (ERNA) found that Schumer’s popularity in New York lags behind Ocasio-Cortez ahead of a potential 2028 challenge. Schumer’s net favorability rating stood at -13 points, while Ocasio-Cortez’s was +8 points across the state, according to the poll. Fifty-two percent of respondents said they view Schumer unfavorably, compared to 39 percent viewing him favorably and 10 percent who didn’t know. Meanwhile, 47 percent of respondents said they viewed Ocasio-Cortez favorably, with 39 percent viewing her unfavorably and 14 percent unsure, according to the poll. It surveyed 505 respondents in New York from August 19 to 21, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. Schumer Has Faced Democratic Backlash Schumer, once a popular figure in the state, has seen diminishing favorability ratings in the second Trump era. He is up for reelection in 2028 and has faced a wave of Democratic backlash over his leadership. Many Democrats have pushed for a more aggressive approach to the Trump administration, though leadership has noted that the party does not control either chamber of Congress and cannot push back on his priorities. Frustration came to a head last year after Schumer helped advance a Republican-backed government funding bill with little fight, yielding no concessions from Republicans. The backlash prompted calls for him to face a primary challenge next year. AOC Favored in Poll, Prediction Markets Over Schumer Ocasio-Cortez has not said whether she plans to run for the Senate, but a poll released last year suggests she would start the primary in a strong position. The poll, conducted by Data for Progress among 767 likely New York Democratic primary voters from March 26 to 31, 2025, showed Ocasio-Cortez with nearly a 20-point lead in a hypothetical 2028 primary matchup between the two. The margin of error associated with the sample size is plus or minus 4 percentage points. Fifty-five percent of respondents said they would pick her over Schumer, while 36 percent said they would stick with the incumbent. An additional 9 percent said they aren't sure who they would vote for. Ocasio-Cortez also leads Schumer on the Kalshi prediction market—she had a 46 percent chance of winning the Senate nomination against Schumer’s 34 percent chance as of Thursday. On Polymarket, however, traders believed she would run for president, not Senate, giving her a 62 percent chance of seeking the presidential nomination. Prediction markets let traders buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real-money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment in the moment but do not always predict the future accurately. Progressive Surge in New York In 2028, the left will work to capitalize on its momentum from the 2026 midterms to expand its power in New York, which has become the heart of the progressive movement over the past few years. Ocasio-Cortez's 2018 victory began a shift in the state, and progressives have made further inroads since. The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) have become major power players in state politics, with their candidates winning numerous primaries for state office in 2026. At the federal level, three progressives—Darializa Avila-Chevalier, Brad Lander, and Claire Valdez—won congressional primaries in New York City. Avila-Chevalier and Lander did so by defeating more moderate incumbents. Avila-Chevalier and Valdez are both members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). DSA also scored a major win with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's victory in the 2025 mayoral race. Mamdani has become another leading face of democratic socialism in the nation's largest city. Could AOC Run for President? Ocasio-Cortez has not ruled out running for president. Many on the left view her as the natural heir to Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, who occupied the progressive lane in the 2016 and 2020 presidential elections. Ocasio-Cortez addressed presidential speculation in May in a conversation with David Axelrod, who served as an adviser to former President Barack Obama. "My ambition is to change this country,” she said. “Presidents come and go. Senate, House seats, elected officials come and go. But single-payer healthcare is forever. A living wage is forever, workers' rights are forever, women's rights, all of that, and so anyways...to a finer point to your question is that when you aren't attached, when you haven't been like fantasizing about being this or that since the time you were 7 years old, it is tremendously liberating." On Thursday, Politico reported that Mamdani, a democratic socialist and close ally of Ocasio-Cortez, signed a petition from the DSA describing her as “the most viable left contender for president in 2028,” though he has not publicly endorsed her. Typically, candidates begin announcing presidential campaigns after the midterms, so it’s possible some contenders could begin announcing later this year or early in 2027. Some progressives view the Senate race as a safer option for Ocasio-Cortez, particularly given the rise of the left in the Empire State. Not all Democrats are sold on Ocasio-Cortez as a presidential candidate, as many believe a more centrist candidate without DSA affiliations could stand a better chance at winning over moderate and independent voters against a Republican candidate. AOC’s Chances in Democratic Primary: What Polls Show Polls suggest Ocasio-Cortez would be a handful of leading contenders alongside prominent Democrats like former Vice President Kamala Harris, California Governor Gavin Newsom, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff and Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro. Here's what two recent polls show about Ocasio-Cortez’s chances of winning in 2028 if she runs for president: HarrisX (August 28-30, 2,100 registered voters, MOE +/- 2.1 points) Quantus Insights (August 26-28, 515 likely voters, MOE +/- 3.2 points) What Happens Next Ocasio-Cortez will be closely watched as a potential candidate for both the Senate and presidential races. The primaries are still more than a year away, so she has plenty of time to make her decision before any formal filing deadlines. However, other candidates could begin announcing presidential runs in the coming months, which could create political pressure not to wait too long to enter the race or risk losing early momentum. news.summary: Some Democrats want Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to challenge Chuck Schumer for his Senate seat in 2028.

news.title: Mike Johnson Just Made the Case for Expanding the Supreme Court
news.text:
Speaker of the House Mike Johnson led an effort Wednesday to amend the Constitution and cap the number of Supreme Court justices at nine. Since the size of the court is currently set by federal law, not by the Constitution, Johnson said the amendment was necessary to stop Democrats from adding justices to the court. Over the course of 24 hours, Johnson announced his plan to introduce the amendment and had it brought to the House floor, only for it to immediately fail along party lines. Despite this defeat, the debate over the court’s structure is just getting started. And Johnson’s “Stop the Count” strategy proves just how much reform is needed.

It doesn’t take a brain surgeon (or even a lawyer) to understand why the leader of the House GOP would like to keep in place a Supreme Court with six Republican appointees. But these kinds of legislative efforts are extremely rare coming from any speaker. Although it was Arizona Rep. Andy Biggs who formally introduced the resolution, Wednesday marked the first time in 30 years that a House speaker has led the charge on proposing a constitutional amendment. What’s more interesting, then, is not the proposal itself, which consisted of only a sentence, but the reason Johnson felt the need to introduce the measure in the first place.

His main rationale is that the Constitution allows Congress to set the size of the court through legislation. Early on in American history, there were often only six justices, a number that Congress expanded periodically. The court’s size rose to 10 by around the Civil War and the creation of the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which covers the Mountain West states. The Judiciary Act of 1869 set the current size at nine. In short, the only thing stopping court expansion is a Democratic congressional majority willing to pass a single court-reform law and a Democratic president willing to sign it.

And as New York Times columnist Jamelle Bouie put it recently, “Democrats are getting serious about court reform.” Former Vice President and Democratic nominee Kamala Harris has officially advocated for expanding the court from nine to 13 justices. A lawyer herself, Harris notes that because the country already has 13 intermediate courts of appeal, a 13-member Supreme Court would allow each justice to review motions from a lower court one-to-one. Former Secretary of Transportation and 2020 Democratic presidential candidate Pete Buttigieg has made the same 13-member argument in his long-running calls to expand the court, while also developing new rules to make the nomination process less partisan. And in an interview this week on Meet the Press, influential South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn noted support for court expansion. So a position that was once shared by only a handful of congressional politicians is now the dominant Democratic view.

Helping the party’s cause is the Constitution, which already gives Congress immense control over the size and structure of the court. Article 3 declares that there must be a Supreme Court, but that it has authority to decide only a narrow category of cases, such as lawsuits between different states. All other types of cases are in the court’s purview merely because Congress decided to grant jurisdiction over that subject by passing a law. The people’s representatives also have the authority to make as many lower federal courts as they choose; Congress has steadily expanded that number as the country has increased in population, to the point that we now have 94 such courts. Finally, the Senate too plays a major role in determining which nominees get confirmed and removed.

In some ways, because of the power of Congress over the courts, there are many reasonable and accessible avenues toward improving our judiciary.

But Republican legislators would rather sabotage their own chamber’s constitutional authority than allow Democrats the chance to reform the court. In opposition to Johnson’s proposal, House Minority Whip Katherine Clark noted that the amendment would strip Congress of “yet another constitutional authority that is meant to be controlled by the American people’s representatives.” Think for a second about the moral calculus the GOP is doing. We’re talking about a system of congressional authority over the court that has lasted for 250 years. And Republicans are so scared of the electorate voting for judicial reform that they would eliminate a key piece of that century-old authority in the two months before they’re likely voted out of office.

Speaking of failing to convince voters, Johnson’s call for constitutional self-castration is shared by his colleagues outside the House—especially those with a history of not getting the votes they want. Texas Sen. Ted Cruz introduced a similarly failed constitutional amendment for the upper congressional chamber last year. The politician, who ran for and lost the Republican nomination in 2016 and candidly stated last week that it’s “no secret that I want to be president,” is a decent standard-bearer for the views of his party as a whole. But before Cruz has another chance at the White House, the party remains led by Donald Trump, the man who sparked an insurrection on the nation’s Capitol after losing the 2020 election. A violent assault on the very same Congress that would vote Wednesday to cement this Trump-friendly court. During that election, Trump notoriously called for election officials to “stop the count!”—but only in the states that temporarily favored him while thousands of ballots were still being counted. Johnson’s approach to freezing the Supreme Court’s current size, right as its Republican nominees reshape American law, has the same antidemocratic aim.

The fact remains that the court-reform debate is raging because we have a high court that is deeply detached from the public. A court committed to implementing the historical will of the long-dead people who first passed a law, while shrugging off the consequences its rulings have on people alive today. A court that avoids contending with ethics complaints against its own members, while blessing ethical violations in the White House. A court that demands the privacy of no cameras in its chambers, while allowing states to invade the private medical decisions of women across the country. A court that anonymously votes behind closed doors in secret rulings, and does so in support of Trump’s not-so-secret effort to disenfranchise votes by mail. Until all of that changes, court reform will be top of mind and top of discussion, no matter what the Republicans try to do before November.
news.summary: The speaker of the house led an effort Wednesday to amend the Constitution and cap the number of justices at nine.
news.author: Alexis Romero

news.title: 'That doesn't concern me': Vance downplays GOP convention no-shows
news.text:
Vice President JD Vance said he's not concerned that some Republicans in key congressional races are planning to skip the party's first-ever midterm convention this month in Texas, downplaying the absences amid questions about whether the event helps battleground candidates.

"That doesn't concern me," Vance said of Republicans opting out of the convention, adding candidates in close races have a lot to juggle, from fundraising to meeting with voters.

"We don't need a congressman in a tight race to be there in all cases," Vance continued. "Sometimes it might be better if that guy's out there raising money. But I think people are going to make a determination: What is the best way for me to spend my time as a candidate."

President Donald Trump is gathering his party for a two-day pep rally in Dallas on Sept. 9 and Sept. 10. Vance is scheduled to speak the first night, and Trump on the second night.

The event has been dubbed "Trumpapalooza" by Republican National Committee Chair Joe Gruters, who said it will help unify the party and reach voters who may not have tuned in yet. Organizers are hoping to boost GOP enthusiasm, but the confab is getting a lackluster reception from some in the party.

A spokesperson for Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, told USA TODAY that she doesn't plan to be at the convention, and instead will remain in her state, a top Senate battleground. Democrat Kamala Harris carried Maine by 7 percentage points in the 2024 election and Collins faces a tough re-election fight.

Meanwhile, a Politico survey of 70 Republican candidates and members of Congress found that most aren't heading to the convention, citing plans in their districts and other obligations.

“I just felt I’d be more useful in my district,” Michigan GOP Rep. Tom Barrett told Politico as he faces a competitive race in a swing seat.

Vance said he and Trump will get much of the media coverage at the convention anyway. Lawmakers in tough contests "should go out there and make the best case they can to their constituents," he said.

Some Republicans are warning the convention could backfire in battleground races.

The event comes just after Labor Day, as the campaign season kicks off in earnest, requiring candidates to take time away from talking to voters less than two months before Election Day. Being too closely tied to Trump also could be problematic for candidates in tight races. Just 4 in 10 voters approve of the president in the Real Clear Politics average of recent polls.

The industry is mourning writer, activist and icon of the feminist movement Gloria Steinem after her death at age 92 was announced on Thursday.

According to posts on her and her foundation’s Instagram accounts, Steinem “passed away peacefully” at her home in New York City “surrounded by many who loved her.“

Recognized as one of the leading figures in the feminist movement, Steinem was active in both politics and media to advance her causes. As a journalist in her early career, she penned political columns and features for New York magazine, with additional published work in Esquire and The New York Times Magazine. She received an Emmy nomination (shared with David Frost, Buck Henry and others) in 1965 for her work on the series, That Was the Week That Was. She also produced and hosted HBO’s Emmy-winning 1993 child-abuse documentary Multiple Personalities: The Search for Deadly Memories and Viceland’s Emmy-nominated 2016 docuseries Woman.

Steinem presented Meghan with the Ms. Foundation’s Women of Vision Award in 2003. “You all know her many accolades and the way in which she helped shape the world for women and all people – ‘we are linked, not ranked‘ she would tell me, and the bracelet she gave me said exactly that. news.title: How The Left Is Taking Over America’s Reddest State
news.text:
Liberal donors, advocacy groups and corporate interests collectively played a key role in defeating conservatives and Freedom Caucus members and replacing them with left-leaning Republicans in August’s Wyoming primaries. 

Left-leaning Republican donors, pro-business groups and organizations coordinated in an effort to Trojan horse non-conservative candidates under the guise of being Republican to run against Freedom Caucus and Trump-endorsed candidates in the Wyoming primaries. The entities spent heavily on the primaries to oppose Freedom Caucus members such as Wyoming state House Speaker Chip Neiman, who lost his state Senate bid to a lesser-known opponent, and Republican Wyoming gubernatorial candidate Eric Barlow, who defeated his Trump-backed opponent, Megan Degenfelder, after being supported by anti-Freedom Caucus donors and groups. 

The Wyoming Freedom Caucus lost its majority in the state House after 13 incumbent members were defeated and four additional Freedom Caucus-aligned members lost their state Senate bids in the August primary. 

Neiman told the Daily Caller News Foundation that activists, such as The Wyoming Donor Alliance, “did everything they could” to turn Wyoming blue by ousting conservatives. 

“Their whole focus was to undo and to do away with the Freedom Caucus and the conservatives,” Neiman said. “I mean, an unbelievable amount of organization dollars are tied into the media, Wayne Hughes [of] Cowboy State Daily, major donors and supporters of this whole thing … It just blew me away as they were relaying this information of the length and the depth and the spider web of connections that just happened and we saw the results of it. But it’s been over time. They really created an incredible machine to do away with the Freedom Caucus and stop conservatives from keeping Wyoming or taking Wyoming in a conservative direction.” 

Activist Orgs Constructed Plan To Defeat Freedom Caucus 

The Wyoming Donor Alliance, a non-partisan organization, outlined a plan to oust Freedom Caucus and Trump-endorsed candidates to replace them with less conservative Republicans. It created a coalition strategy titled, “Break the Wyoming Freedom Caucus Majority,” according to documentation obtained by the DCNF. The organization planned to win back the state House of Representatives by “preventing the spread of extreme Freedom Caucus policies nationwide,” according to the document. (RELATED: ‘James Bond Is Not Real Life’: GOP Candidate Talks Gun Rights, Wyoming’s Water Wars)

The Wyoming Donor Alliance outlined a plan to raise $839,500 to recruit candidates, target specific voters and endorse or oppose candidates, according to the document. They also planned to launch an “unprecedented independent expenditure campaign” ahead of the primaries to oust Freedom Caucus members. 

The organization aimed at recruiting competitive candidates to hold Freedom Caucus members accountable and encourage Republican voters who were not “far-right” to turn out. 

“The Wyoming Donor Alliance is an alliance of donors from across Wyoming who are committed to strengthening voter education, turning out voters, and increasing political accountability,” the organization told the DCNF. “In recent years, our alliance has grown increasingly concerned by the destructive impact Freedom Caucus members were having on our communities and the future of our state. From unconstitutional cuts to education funding and threats to public lands, to the lack of compassion in the face of rural health clinics shuttering and the loss of OB-GYNs and others needed to support infant and maternal health, the Freedom Caucus has created more problems than solutions.”

Americans for Prosperity (AFP), a libertarian-leaning, pro-business advocacy group, endorsed Neiman’s opponent, Republican Wyoming state Sen. Ogden Driskill, a self-described “Reagan conservative” who has been in office in the state Senate since 2011. Driskill ran as the pro-business incumbent and accused the Freedom Caucus of being “very anti-business,” according to Cowboy State Daily. 

“The Freedom Caucus has been very anti-business across the board,” Driskill said. “Doesn’t matter if it’s bringing rodeo to Wyoming; if it’s supporting rare earths up in our district. You know, the Business Council, across the board — they fought data centers.”

AFP-Wyoming told the DCNF that Neiman and other members of the Freedom Caucus became too populist and voted against several important pieces of legislation. A spokesperson clarified that the organization does not support or endorse candidates based on their affiliation with a caucus and that they supported Freedom Caucus members in the past. 

The organization spent about $286,000 in the primaries and endorsed non-Freedom Caucus-aligned candidates. The organization endorsed Republican Wyoming state Sen. Evie Brennan, Republican state Rep. J.R. Riggins and three other Republican candidates running for a seat in the state Legislature. 

One of the endorsed candidates, Jessica Crowder, defeated Freedom Caucus incumbent Ann Lucas. A pro-Freedom Caucus PAC, Make Liberty Win, spent money opposing Riggins as an enemy of the caucus as he ran against Neil Jeske, who was seen as a Freedom Caucus-aligned candidate. Riggins defeated Jeske in the Aug. 18 primary. 

Wyoming is the most Pro-Trump state in the nation. He won it by more than 40 points, 71.60% to 25.84%.Yet, state senator Eric Barlow stomped Trump-endorsed Megan Degenfelder, making her the fifth gubernatorial candidate endorsed by the president to be defeated in primaries. pic.twitter.com/rnFCWFJBHW— Rich Baris THE PEOPLE'S PUNDIT (@Peoples_Pundit) August 19, 2026

Democrat State Lawmaker Opens Wallet For Opponents Running Against Freedom Caucus Candidates

Democratic Wyoming state Rep. Liz Storer, the president and CEO of the George B. Storer Foundation, made personal donations totaling $5,500 to several candidates, including Republican Wyoming state Rep. Doug Moore, who defeated Freedom Caucus member John Bear, according to WyoFile. 

Bear focused on aggressively cutting property taxes, restricting funding on surgeries for trans-identifying minors and passing pro-life legislation. Moore, a newcomer in politics, focused more on fiscal issues and did not campaign heavily on conservative social issues. 

Storer made another personal donation to Republican Secretary of State candidate Robert Short, who defeated Freedom Caucus-aligned state Rep. Rachel Williams in the primary, according to WyoFile. 

New PACs Oppose Freedom Caucus Candidates

Some newly formed political action committees (PACs) spent money to replace Freedom Caucus members. Common Sense Republicans for Wyoming, an issues-based PAC formed in March, spent over $95,000 to oust Freedom Caucus-aligned members, according to WyoFile. 

Common Sense Republicans for Wyoming released a 2026 Republican Primary Voter Guide in July. The PAC endorsed Republican Wyoming gubernatorial candidate Eric Barlow, Short and three candidates running against Freedom Caucus members in the House. Emily Madden, a co-founder of the PAC, touted that 29 out of the 34 candidates they endorsed won their races, according to the Wyoming Tribune Eagle. 

Make Liberty Win, a Virginia-based PAC aligned with the Freedom Caucus, spent nearly $550,000 on the Wyoming races and had a 87% failure rate, according to Cowboy State Daily. 

Media Mogul Runs Anti-Freedom Caucus Outlet 

Wayne Hughes Jr., the owner of Cowboy State Daily, gave $15,000 to the Civil Leadership PAC, which spent about $200,000 backing non-Freedom Caucus Republicans in the primary, according to Transparency USA. The Civil Leadership PAC backed Short and Barlow, which Neiman and other conservatives argued were not true conservatives. 

The PAC spent $168,000 in expenditures to support Barlow’s gubernatorial bid, $19,000 to support Short and over $4,000 on Republican Wyoming state Rep. Steve Harshman, who won his primary in hopes of becoming the next superintendent of public instruction. Harshman defeated Republican Wyoming state Rep. Tom Kelly, who was backed by the Freedom Caucus, according to Cowboy State Daily. 

Hughes, a billionaire businessman, gave $516,000 to the Wyoming Hope PAC since 2020, the biggest share of the PAC’s money, according to Wyoming News. 

Common Sense Republicans for Wyoming, Cowboy State Daily and Storer did not respond to the DCNF’s request for comment. 

Eric Barlow’s Left-Leaning Voting Record 

Neiman told the DCNF that Barlow, who defeated Degenfelder, proved he was not a conservative through his voting record, particularly on issues pertaining to energy and abortion.

“Eric Barlow is not a conservative,” Neiman told the DCNF. “His voting record does not show that … He’s the establishment candidate, that’s just the facts. [There’s] video of him testifying before Congress in the opposition to our legacy industries, coal and gas. I don’t know how you can be conservative and be fighting against the very things that give us national security, and to be portraying yourself as a conservative in that respect, I think, is impossible with that kind of a record.”

Evidence Based Wyoming’s Doug Gerard wrote that Barlow was affiliated with the anti-coal, anti-oil and anti-gas Powder River Basin Resource Council. In 2013, Barlow reportedly voted with a majority of Democrats 90% of the time and was the sixth most liberal Republican in the House. 

Barlow voted to raise taxes on the oil and gas industry, sponsored an amendment in 2014 to accept Obamacare funding in Wyoming and voted to change the definition of marriage, according to Gerard’s report. 

“Eric Barlow’s campaign presents him as a mainstream conservative Republican. His legislative record tells a more complex story,” Gerard wrote in the report. “He is a substantive legislator with deep expertise in healthcare, genuine engagement with energy policy, and credible Second Amendment credentials. However, his overall voting pattern—particularly his fiscal scores, composite political rankings, and extraordinary defection record—places him firmly in the liberal wing of the Wyoming Republican Party.”

Barlow’s campaign did not respond to the DCNF’s request for comment. 

Barlow voted against a bill to ban abortion after a heartbeat was detected, according to the report. However, he voted for bills that restricted abortions. 

Barlow received more than $1,000 from Rene Hinkle, a plaintiff in lawsuits challenging Wyoming’s abortion ban, according to Cowboy State Daily. A Barlow campaign spokeswoman said the donation and others reflected “what [Barlow] stands for. Which is respectful leadership. And he has a record on that.”

“Eric’s record on life in particular, pro-life legislation, is long,” the spokesperson said. “So I don’t think that a donation reflects anything about his policy. It more reflects his leadership style. Which is a respectful leadership style.”

The gubernatorial candidate made property tax reduction a major centerpiece of his campaign. Gerard’s report cited three instances where Barlow voted against property tax relief when the legislation did not pass by large margins. He voted against a bill in 2019 that would have given seniors property tax exemptions. 

Barlow received over $1.7 million in total contributions, according to Transparency USA. He received over $168,000 in direct donations from the Civil Leadership PAC, $40,000 from Conpac Contractors, $5,000 from the Credit Union PAC, $5,000 from the Lawyers Active in Wyoming PAC and $1,000 from the Union Pacific Corporation Fund for Effective Government, according to Transparency USA. 

Wyoming’s Turn PAC, a federal PAC aligned with Republican Wyoming Rep. Harriet Hageman’s Senate campaign, poured about $1.45 million into opposing Barlow and supporting Degenfelder, Cowboy State Daily reported. Hageman won her Senate primary in August. 

Trump won Wyoming 72.3% to 26.1% against former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. In 2022, former Republican Rep. Liz Cheney lost her primary reelection bid to Hageman by a 30-point margin after sitting on the Jan. 6 Select Committee and voting to impeach Trump in January 2021. She campaigned for Democrats, such as Harris.

news.title: A miscalculated strategy is keeping Democrats out of power: Harvard expert
news.text:
How can Democrats reclaim power during the age of President Donald Trump? The answer to that question lies in this axiom: To shape the future, one must understand history.

For twenty years, Republicans won the popular vote in all but one presidential election. In each contest from 1968 to 1988, the GOP prevailed with nominees Richard Nixon, Ronald Reagan and George H. W. Bush.

Then, in 1992, the Democrats nominated Bill Clinton, and for the next twenty years that party won the popular vote in all but one election. Between 1992 and 2012, Clinton, Al Gore and Barack Obama won more votes than their opponents (in 2000 Gore lost in the Electoral College to George W. Bush after a prolonged post-election controversy).

The most recent three presidential elections, from 2016 to 2024, were those in which Trump either prevailed over a female Democrat (Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris) or lost to a man riding on Obama's coattails (Joe Biden).

For Democrats eager to reclaim national power, this recent history raises an obvious question: What did the Democrats do right between 1992 and 2012 that it failed to do either between 1968 and 1988 or in the Trump era?

If you ask Clinton's top political strategist James Carville and top economic adviser Dr. Robert Shapiro, Democrats' two decade period of dominance can be attributed to Clinton focusing on the economy during his 1992 campaign and then delivering a balanced budget, four large surpluses and nearly 23 million jobs, more than any other president before or since. (As Shapiro recently wrote, Clinton accomplished this as he "convinced Democrats in Congress to double down with larger tax increases for wealthy people, raised the corporate tax rate, increased Medicare taxes for wealthy people, and hiked the federal gasoline tax.")

Democrats' rising democratic socialist wing, by contrast, argues that Clinton tacked to the center on key issues like free trade, criminal justice, welfare reform and allowing homosexuals to openly serve in the military. They further add that, while this centrism allowed Clinton, Gore and Obama to prevail in the past, it ultimately weakened the working class and other marginalized groups so much that the party now must move to the left in order to reclaim the political high ground.

Flash forward to 2026 and this debate continues to roil the Democrats, with profound implications for the future of America. If there is one point demonstrated by Trump's two electoral victories, it's that Democrats cannot win elections merely by being better than Trump. They have to offer a constructive and attractive alternative to what Trump's Republican Party offers the American people. But does that consist of following the legacy of the Clinton/Gore/Obama wing of the party or moving to the left as embodied by Democrats like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT)? Should they stick to the budget-conscious approach of Clintonism or the pro-Medicare for All, pro-basic income, pro-free food and overall robustly democratic socialist approach seen in Mamdaniism?

To explore this subject, I spoke with Dr. Theda Skocpol, a Harvard University professor who is Dean of the Graduate School of Arts and Sciences and Director of the Center for American Political Studies. She has also written classic books including "States and Social Revolutions," "Protecting Soldiers and Mothers" and "Diminished Democracy." If there is anyone qualified to contextualize American politics, it is Skocpol.

The following interview has been lightly edited for length, clarity and context.

ROZSA: Do you think Democrats actually agree with the socialist wing in their party?

SKOCPOL: No. For one thing, most people labeled socialists in the media or partisan debates are simply present-day New Deal liberals. They believe in a vigorous welfare state. Now, there are some people, in the Democratic orbit, including a very small number of people who came out of the primaries, who are labeled members of the Democratic Socialists of America. And the Democratic Socialists of America is off there with some pretty weird ideas in the concatenation of things that it supposedly officially endorses. But I don't think that much is going on, except people putting forth vigorous versions of an expanded welfare state on the Democratic Party left.

ROZSA: I think that's a very interesting way of phrasing it, and I think that's important as well. So my next question is: every election year, we see a struggle on issues and outcomes between traditional and more moderate Democrats and economic progressives. We're often told by progressives that Americans agree with them on the issues, but framing like socialism and democratic socialists gets in the way. Is it true that the majority of Democrats agree with them on issues like free grocery stores and guaranteed income? And if that's true, how come more of the candidates who propose those measures don't win their elections?

SKOCPOL: Well, you named a couple of issues where I don't think you could make the case that most Americans agree. You could probably make the case that most Americans like the sound of Medicare for All, although when they get a chance to vote for it in state referenda, they don't. I actually think that you gotta back off from this and recognize that politics has two important dimensions. One is issue stance, and that's what the more ideological formations on the left always wanna stress. And in a weird sort of way, they link up with these pollsters who run these polls that go out and people say, "Well, do you care about X? Do you think X is a good idea without offering any trade-offs or context for X?" But most politics is relational. It's about doing things that are meaningful and respected in your networks and peer groups.

And it's also heavily now kind of inflected with nationalized media sensational identity battles. And on the latter front, the so-called democratic socialists and even most of the economic progressives just aren't in the game because they're a group of more privileged people who live in and around metropolitan areas or college towns. They may never have actually sat in a room, with many working-class people and listened to the way they talk or the way they care about things. Or more to the point, they just don't have relationships with them because geographic and social class polarization has become so great in the United States.

ROZSA: That makes a lot of sense, and I'm glad that you offered that clarification. So my next question is, Trump is described by many as a dangerous populist, and we argue that populism largely fuels his power. Do you think populism is also a danger on the left?

SKOCPOL: Well, I question the premise of this question. Am I allowed to say that?

ROZSA: Absolutely.

SKOCPOL: I believe, first of all, Trump is about Trump, and he embraces particular stances if he thinks they'll get him somewhere. And in 2016 and 2024, he made media-advertised promises that he thought were gonna appeal to disgruntled non-metropolitan constituencies. And they did. But we're seeing the real Trump in this second term. He's mainly interested in his own, as they say, vanity projects, but also building just stupendous grift fortunes for people in his family and his immediate networks. And he's delighted to be aligned with the richest mega billionaires and trillionaires who happen to be pushing forms of investment in AI and other tech-fueled stuff that requires government contracts and all kinds of special breaks in government regulation. I mean, that's what he's doing, and that's the real Donald Trump.

ROZSA: That is a very important point. I guess my follow-up then is why is Trump so often mischaracterized as a populist?

SKOCPOL: Well, because most analysts and social scientists — how to put this in a non-insulting way — are bought into the hopeful delusion that popular opinion drives what happens in politics. If you look at actual policy, at actual things governments do, I don't believe that's more than partially true. And so it is true that especially in his rise and in his surprising reelection, after all that happened, he had blue-collar support, although it's defined mostly as people without college degrees, which I think is not exactly a class definition. It's more of a status definition. He had those votes in elections where he made promises that were lies, essentially, and I think he knew they were. I think he's savvy. I don't think he's stupid.

I think he knew they were lies. And I don't think that means that the people who bought those lies, especially in a media system where they may hear nothing but supposed facts supporting those lies, can be attributed to the driving force of Trumpism. I see Trumpism as much more of a concatenation. And in that concatenation, this charlatan, who's not an unknown figure in American culture and politics, has been pivotal.

ROZSA: So the second part of my question was, is populism also a danger on the left? What are your thoughts there?

SKOCPOL: Well, I don't know what populism is, but if it means paying attention to the needs and hopes and values — I wanna include values in that — of ordinary working people, people who are working for a living for wages and salaries, I don't think it's a danger. I don't think we have much of it, actually. And just proclaiming yourself as a populist, or as some of the democratic socialists do, doesn't change the fact that in many cases they come from and get their votes almost entirely from college-educated factions. Now, I'm part of a college-educated faction myself, so I'm not saying we don't count, but that's a very strange form of populism.

ROZSA: Okay. So my next question is about how do you solve the elephant in the room in terms of how robots have been taking blue-collar factory jobs for decades, and now we're on the cusp of them taking the majority of white-collar jobs in terms of AI. How do we solve for that, especially in terms of what you know about previous issues like this in American economic history?

SKOCPOL: Well, when things spread into the middle class, you're gonna get a political explosion. And that's what's happening now. I think we're at the early stages of it. I have no idea how it's gonna play out because it's happening at a time when faith in government's ability to do things effectively, to create regulatory frameworks for capitalist processes, is at an all-time low, and deservedly so. We just don't have a lot of examples of effective governance in this sphere and many others, including world affairs, that we really need at this point. The United States is in trouble because we just don't have a politics and a governance capable of supporting managed change. And this is a big one.

ROZSA: Now, that brings up a very interesting possibility. Is capitalism still a workable system?

SKOCPOL: Well, we have to make distinctions. I am not convinced that we have. I'm not quite sure what you mean by capitalism, but the definition would be free-market competition. And we haven't had that in the United States for a very long time. We've had regulated capitalism, and now we're devolving into patrimonial corrupt capitalism, which is barely capitalism. I mean, we have a system right now in which our leading-edge business entrepreneurs are really settling for a system of carrots and sticks in which they contact the ruler to get favors and exceptions. And those favors take the form of government contracts, especially. So that's not unheard of in the United States. I mean, a lot of what came out of the Civil War was a government contracting system that was fully exploited by the robber barons.

And now we've got capitalism on steroids. So I don't know how capitalist a system it is, but I think there are a lot of people out there who wanna say capitalism versus socialism. And I think if they say that, they're kidding themselves. Because I think a lot of them, ordinary Americans, have no idea what those abstractions really mean. And they also are gonna say, "Well, if what we've got right now is capitalism," which by the way, I personally analytically don't think it is in any pure form, "if what we've got now is capitalism, I'll take the other one."

ROZSA: So my next question refers to the movie "Primary Colors." There's a scene in that film where the Bill Clinton analog is talking about concerns regarding jobs being outsourced and the loss of manufacturing in the United States. And there's a quote he says that I've always thought was weirdly insightful, and I'm curious if you agree. He said, “Here's the truth: No politician can reopen this factory or bring back the shipyard jobs or make your union strong again,” Stanton says. “No politician can make it be the way it used to be, because we're living in a new world now. A world without economic borders. A guy can push a button in New York and move a billion dollars to Tokyo in the blink of an eye. And in that world, muscle jobs go where muscle is cheap, and that is not here. So if you want to compete, you're gonna have to exercise a different set of muscles, the one between your ears.” And then he proposes affordable lifetime education so that American workers can be trained for the jobs actually being created in this country.

Do you think that is still a plausible rebuttal to the Trump argument about bringing back manufacturing jobs through high tariffs?

SKOCPOL: Well, it's certainly a totally plausible rebuttal to that lie of a promise. I think we need to be careful because I don't buy the idea that the only choice is bring back the 1950s factory jobs versus constantly put people through retraining programs. Think about that for a minute. How appealing would you find that? We have a much more service-based economy now, and we have all kinds of community and public needs that could be met through workers who cannot be replaced by AI. So there are plenty of things we could do to invest in new, community-relevant, as well as economically viable, forms of work, and family life melded with work. I don't know whether we're gonna do that, but it is certainly true that anybody who says the factory jobs, the mining jobs, are coming back is totally out to lunch.

And at this point, we're at the point where a lot of the jobs middle-class people took to sustain themselves are threatened.

ROZSA: All right. And now my last question is: is there anything important that you'd like to say that I haven't given you a chance to say with the questions I've asked so far?

SKOCPOL: Well, it's just to realize that any big political phenomenon, certainly Trumpism, is a coming together of separate strands that may be quite odd combined, but it's the combination that has the power. And I do think that combination was an evisceration, especially of the Republican Party, by wealth holders who wanted little from government except contracts and no taxes and no regulation. They also believed that Trump was appealing to people who were afraid of ethnic changes and racial changes and generational changes in this country, and they were afraid of those things and resentful about the hollowing out of so many communities outside the big cities. But that combination came together to fuel the rise of Trumpism, and now it's coming apart because the whole top-down part of that has turned into the most blatant kind of wealth over regulation of government spending and actions through Trumpist patrimonialism.

Patrimonialism is the oldest form of rule in the world, and it is now melded with the newest kinds of technologies and inequalities.

news.title: Constitutional Amendment to Prevent Democrats From Packing the Supreme Court Fails in the House
news.text:
A Republican sponsored constitutional amendment aimed at preventing Democrats from packing the Supreme Court failed to pass in the House on Wednesday.

House Speaker Mike Johnson (LA-4) on Tuesday announced that House Republicans were proposing the amendment. ““We are going to bring a constitutional amendment. It is a bill to amend the U.S. Constitution to ensure that the U.S. Supreme Court remains composed of only nine justices. We will keep the nine,” he said.

However, the amendment failed because it requires a two-thirds vote to pass.

From CBS News:

A Republican-proposed constitutional amendment to limit the Supreme Court to nine justices failed in the House on Wednesday, coming up well short of the two-thirds majority support needed for adoption. The House voted 212 to 206 on a joint resolution to approve the amendment, which was proposed by GOP Rep. Andy Biggs of Arizona. The amendment would require that "the Supreme Court of the United States shall be composed of nine justices consisting of one chief justice and eight associate justices.""It fixes the number of justices at nine permanently, not because nine is a magic number, but because a fixed court cannot be expanded by whoever happens to win the next election," Biggs said during floor debate Wednesday. Amending the Constitution requires a two-thirds majority vote in both the House and Senate and then ratification by three-fourths of the states.It's the latest vote this week that Republicans are using to target the positions of the Democratic Socialists of America as several candidates who embrace its positions are poised to become members of Congress next year. On Tuesday, the House adopted a resolution condemning socialism "in all its forms."The DSA's platform calls to replace the Supreme Court with a "judiciary chosen by and subordinate to Congress." Some Democrats have called for an expansion of the Supreme Court in recent years, including Rep. James Clyburn of South Carolina, who on Sunday voiced his support for expanding the court to 13 justices.

Democrats have ramped up their calls for expanding the Supreme Court over the past decade. It was a response to a long line of rulings that did not go in their favor. news.text:
It may not be surprising that HBO’s new comic book series, Lanterns, is so exceedingly woke after the show’s writer revealed that she spent ten years as a left-wing community organizer for the likes of Democrat politician Karen Bass and race-hustling attorney Ben Crump.

TV writer Vanessa Baden Kelly recently appeared on the New Rockstars podcast with hosts Erik Voss and Jessica Clemons, where she spoke about her experiences writing the comic book series — which has revealed itself to be a rehash of BLM-era preachy messaging. But she also spoke about where she came from before her TV writing career.

Baden-Kelly began her working life as a child actress for Nick Jr. television, where she appeared in Gullah Gullah Island, before spending several seasons as “Kyra Rockmore” on the popular Keenan & Kel show. But after the year 2000, she took about a ten-year break from the entertainment industry and became a left-wing community activist. By 2011, she went back to seeking work as an actress and also as a writer.

Baden Kelly claimed that her acting career stalled when “diversity” started “slipping backwards” around the year 2000.

“I was working for Karen Bass while still trying to audition, but nothing was really moving because we had slipped backwards in the diversity revolution. And so I started to write,” she said.

In another segment, Baden-Kelly claims that she wrote the Lanterns scene where a character was explaining racism to an alien because “it’s 1986 and this lady knows nothing about nothing.”

The podcast’s co host suggests that the alien species which recruits Green Lanterns around the galaxy may not have known much about race relations on Earth because the Rodney King riots had not yet ravaged Los Angeles when this scene occurs — decades after the Civil Rights era. Baden Kelly enthusiastically co-signs his speculation.

The HBO series came under heavy criticism for its third episode in which one of the characters delivers a lecture on “white privilege.” Some viewers suggested the show was not endorsing the beliefs or actions of this character — the mother of John Stewart, a black Green Lantern, who abuses her son for decades to make sure he gets the gig. However, the actor playing John’s father, J.
